c.st: The Little Book of Linear Algebra
c.x:
Highly recommend to anyone struggling with linear algebra to check out Linear Algebra Done Right, by Sheldon Axler. Do always keep in mind that some concepts are very verbose, but truly out of necessity. If you're talking about an N by N matrix, you're naturally going to have to distinguish N^2 different elements.

You can go very far without touching matrices, and actually find motivation on this abstract base before learning how it interops with matrices.

For those who find Linear Algebra Done Right too much to start with, and those who don't get why Strang starts with matrices, I can't recommend more "The dark art of linear algebra" read this first. With this you can then tackle every other book on the topic more easily

c.st: An Intuitive Guide to Linear Algebra
c.x:
I found Linear Algebra Done Right by Axler to be a fantastic theoretical text that makes everything click together from day 1. It's derived from his paper Down with Determinants.

He starts by explaining that linear algebra is about studying the properties of linear transformations over vector spaces, and then goes on to explain what this means. In many theoretical books it takes ages to get this message, and in some practical ones you get lost in a sea of matrices without even understanding what a matrix actually…

c.st: Ask HN: How or where to begin learning mathematics from first principles?
c.x:
If he's looking for a more of an actual first principles approach to linear algebra, I could not recommend starting with Linear Algebra Done Right by Sheldon Axler enough.

It starts from a few basics which most people would be comfortable with post calculus, and builds up to the most important theorems in linear algebra. It's probably not the book for you if you are actually interested in linear algebra algorithms.

c.st: Mathematicians are chronically lost and confused
c.x: If you're past calculus, I'd say start with Sheldon Axler's Linear Algebra Done Right (it has the most immediate applications, and linear algebra is essential for almost all higher mathematics).

c.st: Summary of MIT's Linear Algebra. Lecture 3: Matrix Multiplication and Inverses
c.x:
There are two introductionary books on linear algebra I would recommend. "Linear Algebra Done Right" by Axler gives you a _very_ nice and rigorous way to the foundations (this text requires a small bit of mathematical maturity, so be aware).

After reading Axler's book you should go and grab a copy of Strang's "Introduction to Linear Algebra" to view the applied side of linear algebra (this is the book mentioned in the article).

c.st: Ask HN: How do you overcome feeling completely lost in life?
c.x:
Tolstoy's Confession is a short yet quite thoughtful read that I'm glad I happened to stumble on many years ago. I'm due for a reread. Even if you don't agree with the conclusions he comes to in there, you will likely relate to the struggles he shares.

Herman Hesse's Siddhartha gave me a somewhat similar feeling after finishing it, which I'm also overdue for a reread.
